---
title: "Indexing"
subtitle: "The full grammar for choosing wells, rows, columns, batches, and quadrants"
---

Most of what you do with a plate is *choose a subset of it*: "these eight wells", "this column",
"every other row". PLR's indexing grammar is deliberately small, and it is worth learning once,
because every pipetting recipe from here on is built on it.

## Setup {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: cell-setup
#| output: false
from pylabrobot.liquid_handling import LiquidHandler
from pylabrobot.liquid_handling.backends import LiquidHandlerChatterboxBackend
from pylabrobot.resources import STARLetDeck, PLT_CAR_L5AC_A00, cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb

lh = LiquidHandler(backend=LiquidHandlerChatterboxBackend(), deck=STARLetDeck())
await lh.setup()

carrier = PLT_CAR_L5AC_A00(name="carrier")
lh.deck.assign_child_resource(carrier, rails=10)
carrier[0] = plate = cor_96_wellplate_360uL_Fb(name="sample_plate")
```

::: {.column-margin}
**Python you need here**

Slices (`"A1:H1"`), `__getitem__` (the `plate[...]` spelling), comprehensions
(`[w for w in ...]`), and generators (`traverse` yields on demand). If a loop you are writing
walks a grid, there is probably a built-in for it.
:::

---

## Select wells {#select}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

Choose a set of wells in one expression. This table is the whole grammar:

| Expression | Selects | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `plate["A1:H1"]` | wells from A1 to H1 along the plate's fill order | 8 wells (row A) |
| `plate["A1", "B2"]` | exactly the listed wells | 2 wells |
| `plate[0]` | the well at index 0 | 1 well (always a list) |
| `plate[range(5)]` | wells at indices 0–4 | 5 wells |
| `plate[0:5]` | the same, as a slice | 5 wells |
| `plate.get_item((0, 0))` | the well at (row, column) | 1 well |

```{python}
#| label: cell-select
print("A1:H1 ->", [w.name for w in plate["A1:H1"]][:3], "... (8 total)")   # <1>
print("A1,B2 ->", [w.name for w in plate["A1", "B2"]])                     # <2>
print("0     ->", [w.name for w in plate[0]])
print("(0,0) ->", plate.get_item((0, 0)).name)      # row A, column 1
```

1. A colon is a *range*: every well from the first identifier to the second, in fill order.
2. A comma-separated list is an explicit set. Note the outer brackets — `plate["A1", "B2"]`.

[**Why it works.** `__getitem__` always returns a list, even for a single well. That is deliberate:
pipetting calls take a list of resources and a list of volumes, so `plate["A1"]` slots straight into
`lh.aspirate(...)` without a special case.]{.why}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gotcha: `plate[(0, 0)]` is *not* row, column

A tuple is treated as a sequence of integer indices, so `plate[(0, 0)]` returns **two copies of
index 0** — a silent bug that duplicates wells. For row, column use `plate.get_item((0, 0))`,
which returns one well. This asymmetry is confusing and it is worth knowing cold.
:::

**See also:** `plate["A1:E1"]` uses the same colon syntax as Python slices; `get_items(...)`
accepts the same identifiers.

:::

---

## Rows and columns {#rows-cols}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

Get one full row or column, or pull wells by index.

```{python}
#| label: cell-rows-cols
print("row(0)   ->", len(plate.row(0)), "wells:", [w.name.split('well_')[1] for w in plate.row(0)][:3], "...")
print("row('A') ->", len(plate.row("A")), "wells")   # row() accepts the label too
print("column(0)->", len(plate.column(0)), "wells:", [w.name.split('well_')[1] for w in plate.column(0)])
```

[**Why it works.** `row()` and `column()` are the two axis views of the same grid. They are
convenience wrappers over `get_item((row, col))` — one call each, no comprehension needed. `row()`
takes an index *or* a letter; `column()` takes an index.]{.why}

::: {.callout-note}
## Which to reach for

Use `row()`/`column()` when the *shape* of what you want is a line. Use the `#select` grammar when
it is not. The overlap is fine — `plate.row("A")` and `plate["A1:A12"]` are the same set by
different names.
:::

**See also:** `get_items(["A1", "A2"])` returns exactly the listed wells — the non-range form of
the comma syntax above.

:::

## Walk a plate in batches {#traverse}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

Hand eight-channel operations a stream of columns, one batch at a time.

```{python}
#| label: cell-traverse
for batch in plate.traverse(batch_size=8, start="top_left", direction="right"):
    first, last = batch[0].name.split("well_")[1], batch[-1].name.split("well_")[1]
    print(f"batch of {len(batch)}: {first} .. {last}")
    if len(batch) == 8:
        break                                        # <1>
```

1. `traverse` is a generator: batches are produced lazily and only when you ask. Iterating the
   whole plate would print all twelve batches.

[**Why it works.** `traverse(batch_size, start, direction, repeat)` walks the plate in fill order
starting from `start` (`"top_left"`, `"bottom_right"`, ...), handing back fixed-size batches. The
`"snake_down"` directions alternate rows — go down column 1, up column 2, and so on — which is the
motion real multi-channel heads like. With `repeat=True` the last (short) batch wraps back to the
start instead of being short.]{.why}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gotcha: the signature is `traverse(batch_size, start, direction)`

Older docs show `traverse(direction, batch_size)`. In 0.2.2 `batch_size` comes first and **`start`
is required** — omit it and you get `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'start'`.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Streaming without a loop**

`repeat=True` turns the generator into an endless cycle — pair it with `itertools.islice` for a
clean "first 20 wells" without writing a counter.
:::

```{python}
#| eval: false
import itertools
first_five = list(itertools.islice(
    plate.traverse(1, "top_left", "right", repeat=True), 5))
```

**See also:** the batching helpers in [chapter 7](../part2/07_worklists.qmd) chunk worklists
across channels the same way.

:::

## Map 96 wells into a 384-well quadrant {#quadrant}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

You have a 384-well plate and an 8-channel head. Aspirate from the wells that correspond to one
96-well quadrant of it.

```{python}
#| label: cell-quadrant
from pylabrobot.resources import biorad_384_wellplate_50uL_Vb

plate384 = biorad_384_wellplate_50uL_Vb(name="dense_plate")       # <1>
carrier[1] = plate384

q1 = plate384.get_quadrant("tl")                                  # <2>
print("top-left quadrant:", len(q1), "wells")

qb = plate384.get_quadrant("br", quadrant_type="block")           # <3>
print("bottom-right block:", len(qb), "wells")
```

1. A 384-well plate — the quadrant grammar only means something on one. On a 96-well plate
   `get_quadrant` still works, but a "quadrant" is then 24 wells and maps to nothing standard.
2. The default `quadrant_type="checkerboard"` interleaves wells the way a 96-in-384 mapping
   physically arranges them — every other well in each direction. All 96 wells of one quadrant.
3. `quadrant_type="block"` takes a contiguous corner instead — also 96 wells, but a solid 8×12
   block. You choose by how the source plate was seeded, not by taste.

[**Why it works.** A 96-well pattern occupies a 384-well plate as a 2×2 checkerboard of
identically-colored positions; `get_quadrant` returns exactly the wells of one color. This is the
indexing feature that makes a 384 plate usable with 8-channel hardware without hand-writing the
pattern.]{.why}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gotcha: quadrant names are compass points, not numbers

`get_quadrant` takes `"tl"`, `"tr"`, `"bl"`, `"br"` (or the long forms). `"Q1"` raises
`ValueError`. The return is a plain list, not a plate — index it like one, but do not expect
`plate[...]` grammar on it.
:::

**See also:** `quadrant_internal_fill_order="column-major"` vs `"row-major"` controls the order
within a quadrant; defaults are sensible for most cases.

:::

## Convert between labels and indices {#labels}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

Turn `"C7"` into `(2, 6)`, or `7` into `"H"` — the plumbing behind every well-ID conversion.

```{python}
#| label: cell-labels
from pylabrobot.resources.utils import row_index_to_label, label_to_row_index, split_identifier

print("row_index_to_label(7):", row_index_to_label(7))   # "H"
print("label_to_row_index('C'):", label_to_row_index("C"))  # 2
print("split_identifier('B12'):", split_identifier("B12"))  # ("B", "12")
```

[**Why it works.** Well labels are base-26 letters with a 1-based column number, which is exactly
the format spreadsheets use and exactly what is annoying to do by hand. The three helpers split
that work: `split_identifier` separates row letter from column number, and the two `*_to_*`
functions convert each half.]{.why}

::: {.callout-note}
## New in 0.2.2

These are recent additions. If you are porting code from an older PLR, you probably reimplemented
them by hand — replace that with the real thing.
:::

**See also:** `split_identifier` is the primitive behind [chapter 7](../part2/07_worklists.qmd)'s
CSV row validation.

:::

## Print an occupancy map {#summary-map}

::: {.recipe}

### The task

Look at a plate as a grid, marking which wells have liquid.

```{python}
#| label: cell-summary-map
for w in plate["A1", "B1", "C1"]:
    w.set_volume(50)                                # <1>

def occupied(well) -> str:
    return "X" if well.tracker.get_used_volume() > 0 else "."

print(plate.summary(occupied_func=occupied))        # <2>
```

1. `set_volume` seeds the tracker directly — a way to tell PLR what is in a well without pipetting
   (see [chapter 11](../part2/11_state.qmd)).
2. `occupied_func` returns **one character per well**; the grid is the payoff. It must return a
   string — returning a bool raises `TypeError`.

[**Why it works.** `summary()` is the same tree-read as [chapter 1](../part1/01_robot_on_screen.qmd#summary)'s
deck view, at well resolution: a 12×8 grid labeled with row letters. The `occupied_func` hook is
where you define "occupied" — liquid, tips, whatever your protocol cares about.]{.why}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Gotcha: the two `summary()` methods are opposites

`lh.summary()` **prints** the deck map and returns `None`. `plate.summary()` **returns** the grid as
a string and prints nothing — which is why this recipe wraps it in `print()`. Forget the `print()`
and the call looks like it silently did nothing.
:::

**See also:** `get_used_volume()` / `get_free_volume()` on the tracker are the volume primitives;
[chapter 10](../part2/10_errors.qmd) covers `TooLittleLiquidError`, which is what makes an
"empty" well fail loudly later.

:::

---

## What to remember

- `plate[...]` always returns a list. Colon is a range; commas are a set; an int is one well.
- **`plate.get_item((row, col))` for row,column — `plate[(row, col)]` duplicates the well.**
- `row()` / `column()` are the axis views; `row()` takes a letter or an index.
- `traverse(batch_size, start, direction)` — `start` is required, and remember `repeat=True` + `islice`.
- `get_quadrant("tl"/"tr"/"bl"/"br")` maps 96→384; checkerboard by default.
- `summary(occupied_func)` prints a grid; the callback returns one character per well.
